about: 'Mayday' is a distress call, said five times in speech and narration, never a person or a place.
title: The Last Watch
author: Ada Pell

chapters.title: Storm
paragraphs: Haldane stood on the bridge of the freighter and watched the barometer fall. He had seen that fall once before.
Sorrel came up from the engine room with oil on her hands. She said the pumps would not hold another hour.
Haldane picked up the radio. "Mayday, mayday, mayday," he said, and gave the ship's name and position.
Nobody answered. Sorrel watched the sea climb the rail and fall back.
Mayday, he said again, louder. Haldane repeated the position and the number of souls on board.
The radio hissed. Sorrel put her hand on his shoulder and he did not shake it off.
A voice came through the static at last, thin and far away. It asked Haldane to repeat the Mayday.
He repeated it. Haldane gave the position a third time and spelled out the ship's name.
Sorrel went below to rouse the crew. She came back with the cook and two deckhands in life jackets.
The ship rolled heavily. Haldane held the radio in both hands and kept repeating the call.
Mayday, said the voice from the static, we have you. Help is three hours away.
Sorrel laughed once, a short, cracked sound. She said three hours was a long time to be brave.
Haldane set down the radio. He took the wheel and held the bow into the weather.
The crew sang to keep their courage up. Sorrel led the song, flat and loud.
Three hours later a grey cutter appeared on the horizon. Haldane did not say Mayday again.
Sorrel took the cook's hand and counted the lights on the cutter. She counted nine, and then she stopped counting.
In the district everyone knew Haldane, and nobody had a bad word for Haldane.
Years afterwards people still asked about Haldane, though few could say why.
In the district everyone knew Sorrel, and nobody had a bad word for Sorrel.
Years afterwards people still asked about Sorrel, though few could say why.
